summary: Global wind patterns for ages 11–13: how uneven solar heating plus Earth's rotation together produce the three circulation cells per hemisphere (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°), the surface wind belts they generate (trade winds, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies), the apparent Coriolis deflection (rightward in the Northern Hemisphere, leftward in the Southern), and the high-altitude jet stream that steers weather systems along it. Core target is NGSS MS-ESS2-6 'develop and use a model': build the pattern from two drivers (heating contrast and spin) rather than only labelling a finished diagram, and connect descending dry air at ~30° to the world's great deserts and rising equatorial air to rainforests, with jet-stream waviness/Arctic amplification as a debated extension linked to prolonged extreme weather.
misconceptions: Thinking the Coriolis effect is a real sideways force pushing the air, rather than an apparent deflection from viewing motion on a spinning planet (and the myth that it determines which way sinks/toilets drain — far too small at that scale).
Believing air simply flows in one straight loop from equator to pole; missing that rotation splits it into three cells per hemisphere.
Assuming winds are named for where they blow TO; in fact winds are named for the direction they come FROM (a 'westerly' blows from the west).
Thinking the equator is hottest because it is closer to the Sun, rather than because sunlight strikes it more directly (higher angle, energy concentrated over less area).
Treating deserts as random hot places rather than the predictable result of descending dry air in the subtropical high-pressure belts at ~30°.

activities.title: Build the planet's circulation from two dials: heating and spin
steps: Starting with the planet's spin set to zero, increase the equator-to-pole heating contrast and observe a single giant convection loop per hemisphere form: warm air rising at the equator, drifting poleward aloft, sinking, and returning along the surface.

Now increase the spin dial up to Earth's rotation rate and observe the single loop break into three side-by-side cells per hemisphere, arranged by latitude, with surface wind belts drawn beneath (trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies).
Use a 'launch a parcel' tool to fire a puff of air poleward and watch its path curve — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern.
Slide a real world map underneath and check where the circulation's branches land: rising equatorial air over the rainforests, descending ~30° air over the Sahara and Australian deserts.

As an extension, toggle a jet-stream ribbon at a cell boundary and observe how this fast high-altitude river of air steers weather systems along its path; then explore a 'wavier jet' slider and reason about what a more meandering, 'stuck' jet might do to the weather beneath it.
activities.insight: Large-scale wind bands are the emergent OUTPUT of two interacting drivers — uneven heating by latitude and the planet's rotation. The single convection loop you expect splits into three cells once spin is added, and the bending of the winds is an apparent deflection that only appears once the planet turns beneath the moving air, not a sideways push.

activities.title: Spin a globe and launch parcels across it (spatial Coriolis)
steps: On a spinnable 3D globe, launch a 'straight' path from the equator toward a pole and watch the trace curve relative to the rotating surface: in both hemispheres, a parcel moving toward the pole arcs eastward. On a physical turntable/lazy-Susan, which stands for one hemisphere seen from above its pole, draw a straight line with a pen across the spinning disc and watch the trace curve.
Compare launches in the Northern Hemisphere (path curves right) and the Southern Hemisphere (path curves left), and say why the two differ.
Peel back or tilt to view the three cells as latitude bands girdling the planet, and view the jet stream as a meandering ribbon from a polar vantage.
activities.insight: Circulation wraps a rotating sphere; seeing a straight-intended path curve on a surface you can spin makes the apparent (frame-dependent) nature of Coriolis concrete, and the opposite deflection in each hemisphere follows from the direction of rotation seen from each pole.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, sequence, predict, and locate
steps: Match each cell to its latitude band (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°) and each surface belt to its wind direction (trade winds easterly/equatorward, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies).
Sequence the causal chain: equator heated most → air rises → drifts poleward → sinks near 30° → returns as surface wind belt.
Given a poleward-launched parcel, draw or select its correctly curved path in each hemisphere (right in N, left in S).
Categorise named regions as wet-equatorial (rising air) or dry-subtropical (descending air at ~30°), e.g. placing the Sahara and Australian deserts under descending air.
Explain in your own words why the equator is hottest — sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating energy over less area — rather than because it is closer to the Sun.
Connect the mid-latitude westerlies to everyday experience: because they blow from the west, weather systems in the UK and US generally move from west to east.
activities.insight: Secure the discriminations after exploring the model: naming cells and belts, predicting deflection direction, locating deserts/rainforests from the circulation, and linking the westerlies to west-to-east weather turn the model into reliable, transferable knowledge.

activities.title: Ask the meteorologist: untangle Coriolis and wind-naming
steps: Pose and discuss whether the Coriolis effect is a real push on the air, and explain in your own words what actually makes a north-bound wind veer right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Ask why 'a westerly' is named for where the wind comes from, and check the drain/toilet-spin claim against the fact that Coriolis is negligible at small scales.
activities.insight: Articulating the explanation aloud and responding to follow-up questions can expose and help repair the Coriolis-as-force and winds-named-from misconceptions that a diagram may leave hidden.

checkQuestion: Winds don't travel in straight lines from the equator to the poles — they curve. A student says 'that's because the Coriolis force pushes the moving air sideways.' Is the Coriolis effect a real push on the air, and what actually makes a north-bound wind in the Northern Hemisphere veer to the right?
checkAnswer: There's no real sideways force pushing the air. The air moves nearly straight, but the Earth rotates beneath it; from our rotating frame the path appears deflected — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. It's an apparent deflection due to Earth's rotation, not a force acting on the air. Combined with unequal heating by latitude, this shapes the three-cell circulation and the prevailing winds.
